result.summary: The Cretan sailors obey Apollo, beach their ship, make an offering at an altar, and follow the god playing his lyre to Parnassus. There they ask how they will live in a barren land, and Apollo tells them to tend his temple and receive worshippers, warning them to stay righteous. The poet then bids farewell to the god.

scenes.title: Landing, offering, and march to Pytho
scenes.summary: The Cretans beach the ship, build an altar and make offerings, then follow Apollo, playing his lyre, to Parnassus and his temple.

scenes.title: Apollo's charge to the Cretans
scenes.summary: The Cretan leader worries that the land cannot feed them. Apollo smiles, promises abundance from offerings, and tells them to guard the temple and keep righteousness or be subjected to other men.
scenes.stakes: The Cretans risk poverty now and, if they prove unrighteous, permanent subjection to other men.

scenes.title: Poet's farewell
scenes.summary: The poet bids farewell to Apollo and promises another hymn.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo's gently mocking rebuke of the Cretans' worry, explaining their new calling.

analysis.text: The passage ends the founding story of Delphi: mortals are given a sacred duty and told that prosperity depends on righteousness.
It reflects how the Delphic sanctuary was sustained by pilgrims' offerings and by priests who were expected to stay honest and impartial.

fun_facts.text: The Ie Paean sung here was a ritual cry associated with Apollo, used in hymns of praise and healing.

language_notes.text: "Sheets" are the ropes controlling the sail's lower corners; "forestays" are ropes running from the mast to the bow. The crew is lowering the mast to rest it.
The "long stays" are props or supports set under the hull so the beached ship stays upright.
"Featly" is an archaic word meaning neatly or nimbly, describing Apollo's graceful stepping.
The "Ie Paean" is a ritual cry and hymn addressed to Apollo, here sung as the Cretans march in step.
Parnassus is the mountain above Delphi, the site of Apollo's sanctuary, which was earlier called Pytho.
"Drudges" are people who do hard, menial labour; Apollo means the Cretans worry needlessly and expect toil.
"Guard you my temple" and "do you keep" are archaic imperatives, meaning "you must guard" and "you must keep."

context_notes.text: Offering barley or white meal on an altar with a fire was a common Greek way to begin worship and ask a god's favour.
Crete was known for its music and paean-singing, which explains why these Cretans are made Apollo's priests.
Hymn poets typically close by greeting the god and promising another song, as happens here.

literary_notes.text: Apollo's lyre-playing and high, graceful step give a vivid picture of the god leading his new priests.
Apollo calls the Cretans foolish for fearing hardship, though he had brought them here; his smile shows divine ease against mortal worry.
The warning that other men will rule them hints at the temple's later troubles if its servants prove corrupt.
The poet turns directly to Apollo with a farewell, a conventional close that links this hymn to the next song.
